newsitem.title: USA: Johnson Controls, UAW resume talks. [CORRECTED 01:45 GMT 12/2]
newsitem.headline: Johnson Controls, UAW resume talks. [CORRECTED 01:45 GMT 12/2]

text.p: Ford Motor Co. said Tuesday it plans to resume production of its hot-selling Expedition full-size sport utility vehicle Wednesday morning in a move that will bring 4,000 employees back to work.
The assembly line at the Michigan Truck Assembly plant in Wayne, Mich., will begin rolling with the normal first shift Wednesday morning, said company spokeswoman Francine Romine-MacBride.

Expeditions made Wednesday, Thursday and Friday will have only front seats installed. They will then be stored while Ford waits for Lear Corp. to ramp up its production of second- and third-row seats.
On Saturday, Ford will begin making Expeditions with all rows of seats and start shipping them to dealers, said Romine-MacBride.

Ford suspended Expedition production, as well as output of Econoline and Club Wagon full-size vans, Friday after it looked like there would not be a quick end to a United Auto Worker strike against Johnson Controls Inc., the regular seat supplier for the vehicles.
On Monday, Ford said it would resume Expedition production with substitute second- and third-row seats from Lear and front seats from its own Chesterfield, Mich., trim plant.

Expeditions are only made at the Michigan Truck plant. The plant normally runs two 10-hour shifts a day, seven days a week, producing 840 of the high-profit Expeditions a day. The company will have lost production of about 3,360 (company corrects from 4,200) Expeditions, which industry analysts have said will be almost impossible to recoup.

Ford also makes five of the popular F-150 pickup trucks an hour at Michigan Truck. That means it missed out on production of about 400 (company corrects from 500) of those vehicles during the shutdown.
The company has not made a final determination on when it will retrofit 7,700 Expeditions made without seats. It has said it will also look into restarting two Econoline production lines in Ohio.
Meanwhile, in what may be a break in the 15-day strike, negotiators for Johnson Controls and the United Auto Workers spoke for several hours late Monday and early Tuesday.
The renewed discussions came hours after Ford said it would restart the Expedition line with seats from Lear, Johnson Control's chief competitor in the auto seat business.
"We're hopeful there will be some additional discussions," said Johnson Controls spokesman Jeff Steiner.

No talks were held later Tuesday, but Steiner characterised the negotiations as being adjourned, compared with previous sessions where talks broke off completely. The two sides had not spoken since late Thursday.

Unable to agree on terms for a new contract, about 500 UAW members at Johnson Controls seat plants in Plymouth, Mich., and Oberlin, Ohio, walked off the job Jan. 28. In addition to the Expedition full-size sport utility, the plants make seats for Ford's Econoline and Club Wagon full-size vans.

In another strike threat to an auto parts maker, the UAW said Tuesday it issued a Friday night strike deadline against American Axle & Manufacturing Inc., the main supplier of truck axles to General Motors Corp.

UAW spokesman Reg McGhee said about 7,500 workers in Detroit, Three Rivers, Mich., and Buffalo, N.Y., will go on strike at 11:59 p.m. EST Friday if company and union negotiators fail to reach a deal for a new labour contract.
